result.requested_outcome: Disease-specific disability measured by the Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ)
result.relation_rationale: The abstract reports disease-specific disability-RMDQ values for antibiotic and placebo at baseline, 100 days, and one year, including 5.7 and 14 at one year as requested. The one-year analysis population is restricted to follow-up attendees (144 of 162 randomized), making this result narrower than the randomized-population target. The detailed table separately reports one-year medians of 7.0 and 14.0, conflicting with the abstract's antibiotic value.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

sections.excerpt: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.

1|ORIGINAL ARTICLE
2|Antibiotic treatment in patients with chronic low back pain
3|and vertebral bone edema (Modic type 1 changes): a double-blind
4|randomized clinical controlled trial of efficacy
5|Hanne B. Albert • Joan S. Sorensen •
6|Berit Schiott Christensen • Claus Manniche
7|Received: 6 August 2012 / Revised: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 15 January 2013 / Published online: 13 February 2013
8| Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2013
9|Abstract
10|Purpose
11|Modic type 1 changes/bone edema in the
12|vertebrae are present in 6 % of the general population and
13|35-40 % of the low back pain population. It is strongly
14|associated with low back pain. The aim was to test the
15|efficacy of antibiotic treatment in patients with chronic low
16|back pain ([6 months) and Modic type 1 changes (bone
17|edema).
18|Methods
19|The study was a double-blind RCT with 162
20|patients whose only known illness was chronic LBP of
21|greater than 6 months duration occurring after a previous
22|disc herniation and who also had bone edema demonstrated
23|as Modic type 1 changes in the vertebrae adjacent to the
24|previous herniation. Patients were randomized to either
25|100 days of antibiotic treatment (Bioclavid) or placebo and
26|were blindly evaluated at baseline, end of treatment and at
27|1-year follow-up.
28|Outcome measures
29|Primary outcome, disease-specific
30|disability, lumbar pain. Secondary outcome leg pain,
31|number of hours with pain last 4 weeks, global perceived
32|health, EQ-5D thermometer, days with sick leave, bother-
33|someness, constant pain, magnetic resonance image (MRI).
34|Results
35|144 of the 162 original patients were evaluated at
36|1-year follow-up. The two groups were similar at baseline.
37|The antibiotic group improved highly statistically signifi-
38|cantly on all outcome measures and improvement continued
39|from 100 days follow-up until 1-year follow-up. At base-
40|line, 100 days follow-up, 1-year follow-up the disease-
41|specific disability-RMDQ changed: antibiotic 15, 11, 5.7;
42|placebo 15, 14, 14. Leg pain: antibiotics 5.3, 3.0, 1.4; pla-
43|cebo 4.0, 4.3, 4.3. Lumbar pain: antibiotics 6.7, 5.0, 3.7;
44|placebo 6.3, 6.3, 6.3. For the outcome measures, where a
45|clinically important effect size was defined, improvements
46|exceeded the thresholds, and a trend towards a dose-
47|response relationship with double dose antibiotics being
48|more efficacious.
49|Conclusions
50|The antibiotic protocol in this study was
51|significantly more effective for this group of patients
52|(CLBP associated with Modic I) than placebo in all the
53|primary and secondary outcomes.
54|Keywords
55|Modic changes Antibiotics Chronic low
56|back pain End plate changes LBP
57|Introduction
58|Modic type 1 changes are bone edema in vertebrae and
59|have been shown to be both commonly observed in and
60|tightly associated with, low back pain [1, 2]. A recent
61|systematic review showed that the prevalence for any type
62|of Modic change in patients with non-specific low back
63|pain (LBP) was 46 % as opposed to 6 % in the general
64|population [1]. A positive association between Modic type
65|and non-specific LBP was found with a mean odds ratios of
66|4.5 [4, 5]. These findings are relevant as chronic lower back
67|pain (CLBP) is seldom reliably attributable to specific
68|pathoanatomical causes [3].
69|Modic changes are only visible on magnetic resonance
70|images (MRI) and three types have been identified (Types
71|1-3) [4]. Histological studies of material harvested during

1|surgery, show that Type 1 involve disruption and fissuring
2|of the endplate with regions of degeneration, regeneration,
3|reactive bone formation, endplate edema and vascular
4|granulation tissue [4, 5]. Several studies have examined the
5|reliability of reporting Modic changes and all have shown
6|excellent inter and intra-observer reliability [6, 7]. In
7|comparative studies, Modic changes have demonstrated a
8|higher reliability than other MRI findings, such as disc
9|herniations [8].
10|Infection is one of the hypothetical causes of the bone
11|edema underlying Modic type 1 changes [9]. Stirling found
12|nuclear tissue removed under strict sterile conditions dur-
13|ing surgery for lumbar herniated discs, to be infected with
14|low virulent anaerobic organisms (Proprionibacterium
15|acnes and Corynebacterium propinquum) in 53 % of the
16|patients [10]. To investigate if skin contamination was the
17|cause of this surprising result, Stirling et al. conducted
18|another study with 207 patients with lumbar disc herniation
19|and 27 patients with other spinal disorders such as scoli-
20|osis, fracture and tumors, all patients had nucleus material
21|removed. In 37 % of the patients with lumbar disc herni-
22|ation bacteria were indentified, mainly P. acnes. Con-
23|versely, no (0 %) bacteria were found in the extracted
24|nuclear material in the group with other spinal disorders. If
25|skin contamination was the cause of the bacterial presence
26|in the nucleus material the percentage of infected patients
27|should be very similar [11]. Corsia et al. [12] replicated this
28|and evacuated extruded disc material in 30 lumbar disc
29|herniations: 71 % were infected, 36 % with Staphylococ-
30|cus and 18 % with P. acnes; and in 30 cervical disc her-
31|niations they found 59 % were infected, 37 % with
32|P. acnes. Agarwal et al. [12] cultured material from 52
33|patients, 10 (19 %) of them were infected and in 7 (70 %)
34|of those, P. acnes was the sole organism isolated. It is
35|thought that these anaerobic mouth and skin commensal
36|organisms gain access to the disc during normal bactere-
37|mias as a result of the neovascularisation associated with
38|disc degeneration or herniation [13-21]. Local inflamma-
39|tion in the adjacent bone may be a secondary effect due to
40|cytokine and propionic acid production, i.e., the infection is
41|in the disc and the Modic change is a ''side effect'' man-
42|ifest in the bone. P. acnes cannot live in the highly vas-
43|cularised/aerobic bone and is not present there [22].
44|To evaluate the role of P. acnes in the occurrence of
45|later Modic type 1 changes after a disc herniation, a cohort
46|study of 61 immunocompetent patients undergoing surgery
47|for a lumbar disc herniation underwent an MRI examina-
48|tion before surgery and 1-2 years afterwards. Evacuation
49|of nuclear material took place during surgery under strict
50|sterile conditions. The study revealed that 46 % of the
51|patients had infected nuclear material, 84 % of these with
52|P. acnes. The possible role of bacteria in developing Modic
53|changes after a disc herniation was confirmed hence, 20 of
54|the 25 (80 %) with anaerobic cultures developed new
55|Modic changes in the vertebrae adjacent to the previous
56|disc herniation, compared to 16 of the 36 (44 %) with no
57|identified infection or aerobic bacterial infection (n = 2).
58|Fisher's exact test p \ 0.0079 [23].
59|In a recently published uncontrolled pilot study, 32
60|patients with chronic low back pain, following a lumbar
61|disc herniation and of up to 2 years duration associated
62|with Modic type 1 changes/bone edema, were treated with
63|Amoxicillin-clavulanate (500 mg/125 mg) 3 9 day for
64|90 days [24]. Twenty-nine patients (90.6 %) completed the
65|treatment and three patients dropped out due to diarrhea. At
66|the end of treatment and at long-term follow-up (mean
67|10.8 months) there was both a clinically important and
68|statistically significant (p B 0.001) improvement in all
69|outcome measures [24]. These results provided additional
70|tentative support for the hypothesis that bacterial infection
71|may play a role in LBP with Modic changes (bone edema).
72|The aim of this study was to test the efficacy of Modic
73|antibiotic spine therapy (MAST) in patients with chronic
74|low back pain, new Modic type 1 changes in the vertebrae
75|adjacent to a previously herniated disc. Additionally, we
76|investigated whether a dose-response relationship could be
77|identified.
78|Methods
79|This clinical trial was conducted at the Spine Centre of
80|Southern Denmark and the participants were recruited from
81|two secondary spine centers. The initial inclusion criteria
82|were: age between 18 and 65 years, MRI-confirmed disc
83|herniation L3/L4 or L4/L5 or L5/S1 within the preceding
84|6-24 months, lower back pain of[6 months duration, both
85|conservative and surgically treated patients were included,
86|regardless of sciatica, neuropathic pain or not. Individuals
87|who fulfilled these criteria were posted a letter describing
88|the project as well as a questionnaire containing pain
89|drawings and the exclusion criteria: allergy to antibiotics,
90|current pregnancy or lactation, any kidney disease or
91|pending litigation. Subjects who fulfilled final criteria and
92|were interested in participation underwent a repeat MRI;
93|all performed at the Spine Center of Southern Denmark
94|(T1- and T2-weighted images). Individuals were then
95|consecutively recruited into the study if their repeat MRI
96|showed Modic type 1 changes adjacent to the previously
97|herniated disc regardless of size of the Modic change.
98|Modic findings were coded by an experienced research
99|radiologist. With regard to the presence and coding of
100|Modic changes, this radiologist demonstrated a perfect
101|intra-tester reliability (kappa = 1.0) and an excellent inter-
102|tester reliability (kappa = 0.93) [25]. The size and volume
103|were graded according to the Nordic Modic Protocol [8]:

1|1 = endplate only, 2 = up to 25 %, 3 = up to 50 %
2|4 = above 50 % of the vertebrae. Patients also had to have
3|LBP in the area from L1 to L5 with a Numerical Pain
4|Rating Scale score of C6 after adding the current LBP
5|(0-10); the mean LBP during the last 2 weeks (0-10) and
6|worst LBP during the last 2 weeks (0-10) and then
7|dividing by three.
8|Randomization was performed by the Central Pharmacy,
9|Odense University Hospital using a computer-generated
10|randomization list retained at the pharmacy until after the last
11|patient's 1-year follow-up. Placebo tablets were calcium
12|carbonate and identical in size, color, coating and aluminum
13|packing to the active tablets. All tablets were packed in sealed
14|white cardboard boxes on which only the patient number was
15|printed (1-162). Patients and the assessor were blinded to
16|randomization until after completion of the patient's 1-year
17|follow-up. Patients were recommended not to seek any other
18|treatment during the 1-year follow-up period. At both follow-
19|up treatments by doctors, physiotherapists and alternative
20|treatment providers were registered.
21|Three independent experts in infectious diseases were
22|presented with the bacterial culture results of Stirling's study
23|[10] and all three recommended amoxicillin-clavulanate.
24|This drug is known to be able to penetrate into the discs [26].
25|Therefore, treatment consisted of amoxicillin-clavulanate
26|(500 mg/125 mg) (Bioclavid ) tablets three times a day, at
27|8 h intervals, for 100 days. This long duration of antibiotic
28|treatment is commonly prescribed for post-operative discitis.
29|The randomization divided patients into four dosage
30|groups: A (n = 45) one Bioclavid tablet, B (n = 36) one
31|placebo tablet, C (n = 45) two Bioclavid tablets, D
32|(n = 36) two placebo tablets. Compliance was measured in
33|daily medication diaries. During their 12-month participa-
34|tion in this trial patients were not provided with any other
35|treatment except mild analgesics, if required.
36|Study flow
37|At both baseline and at 1-year follow-up each participant
38|underwent a physical examination and completed self-repor-
39|ted questionnaires. An MRI and blood samples were also
40|taken. The MRI protocol at baseline and at the 1-year follow-
41|up were uniform and performed by the same staff, blinded to
42|treatment, and in the same MRI machine. At the end of the
43|treatment period, (100 days), patients were also mailed a
44|questionnaire. The patients and the observer were blinded to
45|the allocation and all previous measurements. All physical
46|examinations were performed by the same blinded observer.
47|At baseline, all patients had a 1.5 h thorough patient
48|education session including important information about;
49|what are Modic changes? Why are they so painful? What is
50|the presumed pathoanatomical pathway for the link
51|between the previous herniation and the present Modic
52|type 1 changes? Why they should not do exercise during
53|the treatment period and so forth. All patients were allowed
54|to take their usual anti-inflammatory and pain relieving
55|medication (treatment as usual).
56|To avoid a later need for imputation, the project secre-
57|tary checked every questionnaire for completion, if missing
58|data, the patient was asked to fill in before leaving the
59|center. A project secretary, also blinded to treatment allo-
60|cation, entered all data in EpiData v3.1 (The EpiData
61|Association, Odense, Denmark), coded under the partici-
62|pant's project number.
63|Outcome measures
64|All patients underwent clinical examination and blood tests
65|(serum analysis) at baseline and at end of treatment. Self-
66|reported questionnaires were completed at baseline; end of
67|antibiotic treatment (100 days), and at 12-month follow-up.
68|The outcome measures are presented in Table 1.
69|The primary outcome measures were disease-specific
70|disability Roland Morris Questionnaire [27] (RMDQ) and
71|lumbar pain [28] (LBP Rating Scale). A clinically impor-
72|tant change was defined as a 30 % reduction of the indi-
73|vidual's baseline score and 2 LBP rating scale points [29]
74|(Table 1). Secondary outcome measures were global per-
75|ceived effect, leg pain, hours with LBP during the last
76|4 weeks, EQ-5D Thermometer, days with sick leave,
77|bothersomeness, constant pain, MRI Modic grading, serum
78|analysis, four test at the physical examination.
79|Sample size
80|Power calculations were based on the results of a pilot
81|study, where the patients receiving antibiotics had a med-
82|ian reduction of RMDQ of 3.7 [24]. A sample size of 65 in
83|each group was calculated as necessary to detect a reduc-
84|tion of minimum 3.7 in the antibiotic group on the RMDQ,
85|with a SD of the difference of four and a placebo effect of
86|1.4 on the RMDQ, for an alpha of 0.05 and a power of 0.90.
87|Dropout due to side effects was estimated to be 10 %. The
88|sample size calculation is based on a two-group compari-
89|son hence comparing antibiotics with placebo is the main
90|aim. To fulfill a late request from the Danish Medical
91|authorities a dose-response part was included, but the
92|study is not designed for this tertiary purpose and therefore
93|this is not formally tested.
94|Statistics
95|All statistics were performed by an independent professor
96|in statistics at Aalborg University who was blinded to
97|group allocation. Data were analyzed in STATA version
98|16.

1|Differences in binary variables were tested with Fisher's
2|exact test. Continuous data were analyzed with three tests.
3|Firstly, crude an unpaired T-tests; secondly, adjusted for
4|gender and age. Thirdly, if the distribution was not nor-
5|mally distributed, with the Mann-Whitney test. No interim
6|analysis was performed. Analyses were preformed on all
7|patients who participated at the 1-year follow-up and all

10|Ethics
11|The study was approved by and registered in: the Danish
12|Medicine Agency and the Scientific Ethics Committee of
13|the Region of Southern Denmark (no. S-VF-20050112),
14|the Danish Data registry, Euro-dract (2005-005500-17),
15|Government Clinical trial registry (NCT00302796) and
16|monitored by the Unit of Good Clinical Practice (GCP),
17|University of Southern Denmark. All patients signed a
18|written informed consent prior to participation.
19|Results
20|The study flow chart is shown in Fig. 1. Of the 162 patients

23|follow-up (MRI, questionnaires, physical examination).
24|All baseline variables were equally distributed in the
25|placebo and antibiotic groups (Table 2). The only exception
26|was the volume of Modic changes, where the placebo group
27|had significantly more minute changes (grade 1).
28|There were no significant differences in age and gender
29|between the 1-year participants and those lost to follow-up;
30|however, there were significantly more smokers amongst
31|those lost to follow-up.
32|The antibiotic group improved on all primary outcome
33|measures and improvement continued from 100 days follow-
34|up until 1-year follow-up. In comparison to the placebo group,
35|the 1-year improvement was both statistically significant on all

37|relative magnitude of improvement for the primary outcome

27|healing process that starts only when and after the bacteria
28|have been killed.

30|acid, which has the capacity to dissolve fatty bone marrow
31|and bone. We hypothesize that diffusion of propionic acid

20|Many antibiotics have an anti-inflammatory effect,

34|effect took 6-8 weeks to manifest, more consistent with the
35|clinical course of resolving infection in poorly vascularised
36|infected tissue, i.e., an antibiotic effect.

44|satisfied with their result and therefore sought additional
45|help.

22|The trend favoring double dose antibiotics not reaching
23|significance is likely to reflect a classical type two error,

1|CLBP with Modic type 1 changes. We do not support the
2|proposition that all patients with lumbar pain should have a
3|trial course of antibiotics. The criteria in this study were
4|very clear: CLBP for more than 6 months, Modic type 1
5|changes in the adjacent vertebrae following a previous disc
6|herniation. As we do with other drugs, we rely on our
7|fellow colleagues to use clear evidence-based criteria and
8|to avoid excessive antibiotic use. We also suggest more
9|confirmatory work in other populations, for example,
10|Modic type 2 changes, and studies on improved protocols
11|should be supported.
12|Conclusions
13|In this double-blind RCT patients with CLBP and Modic type
14|1 change (bone edema) following a lumbar disc herniation,
15|who were treated with antibiotics obtained statistically sig-
16|nificant improvements compared to the placebo group in all
17|measured parameters, including: the primary outcome of
18|disease-specific disability, back pain intensity, and the sec-
19|ondary outcomes of, leg pain intensity, general improvement,
20|number of hours with pain, reduced number with chronic
21|pain, physical examination tests, and MRI Modic grading.
22|Only four participants (2.8 %) stopped treatment due to side
23|effects, which were mostly gastroenterointestinal.
24|For the primary outcome measures, the effect size was
25|clinically important in magnitude and substantially greater
26|than all currently established treatments.
27|Antibiotics could be considered as a treatment option for
28|this special subgroup of patients with CLBP and Modic
29|type 1 changes after a lumbar disc herniation when all other
30|treatment options have failed. More confirmatory work in
31|other populations and studies on improved protocols as
32|well as the background science should be encouraged.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
invalid_shortcuts: analysis denominators or ITT membership alone
an event count treated as an observed-outcome count
an analysis denominator treated as an outcome denominator
a generic censoring rule without actual rates or follow-up accounting
imputed data counted as observed outcomes
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

Availability and mitigation are separate premises: a familiar method name or numerically stable estimate is not enough; the sensitivity analysis must span plausible assumptions relevant to the documented missingness mechanism.
This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.
invalid_shortcuts: multiple imputation based only on intervention group
questions.no_information_rule: No_information is not an allowed response to this question in the parallel-assignment pack. Answer no/probably no when inspected evidence does not establish protection from missing-data bias. No does not assert that bias occurred: retain source coverage limits and unknown missingness mechanisms. Ground the scoped negative answer in inspected Evidence or a valid scoped no-hit receipt; an unsupported limitation alone is insufficient.
questions.official_guidance: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

answer_anchors.text: Missingness could depend on the true outcome value.
Documented missingness reasons are unrelated to the outcome.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value.
considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation is not loss to follow-up when outcome ascertainment continues; stopping treatment or an analysis label alone does not establish whether the outcome was observed. Last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.

Withdrawal or censoring after worsening health or symptoms can support possible dependence on the outcome value when the source links the reason to that participant's outcome; stopping treatment without that follow-up loss does not.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when loss to follow-up or withdrawal could relate to health status or outcome. Answer no or probably no when all missingness had documented reasons unrelated to outcome, such as a failed measuring device or interruption to routine data collection.
evidence_needed: Reasons for missingness and their relationship to participants' health status or true outcome, including censoring and treatment switching in time-to-event analyses.
invalid_shortcuts: a reason for withdrawal without its relation to outcome
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the reasons for missingness do not permit assessment of dependence on the true value.
questions.official_guidance: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
questions.wording: If N/PN to 3.2: Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?

answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.
The analysis accounted for characteristics explaining the relationship, or dependence was not likely.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness that could depend on true value likely depended on it.
considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.
questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. Answer no when analysis accounted for participant characteristics likely to explain the relationship.
evidence_needed: Group-specific missingness or censoring, reasons for missingness, trial circumstances, and any analysis accounting for relevant participant characteristics.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of dependence on true value cannot be judged from the available evidence.
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 3.3: Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?

Differences in binary variables were tested with Fisher's
exact test. Continuous data were analyzed with three tests.
Firstly, crude an unpaired T-tests; secondly, adjusted for
gender and age. Thirdly, if the distribution was not nor-
mally distributed, with the Mann-Whitney test. No interim
analysis was performed. Analyses were preformed on all
patients who participated at the 1-year follow-up and all
patients were analyzed in their 'intention to treat' group,
regardless of their compliance to the medicine protocol.
Ethics
The study was approved by and registered in: the Danish
Medicine Agency and the Scientific Ethics Committee of
the Region of Southern Denmark (no. S-VF-20050112),
the Danish Data registry, Euro-dract (2005-005500-17),
Government Clinical trial registry (NCT00302796) and
monitored by the Unit of Good Clinical Practice (GCP),
University of Southern Denmark. All patients signed a
written informed consent prior to participation.
Results
The study flow chart is shown in Fig. 1. Of the 162 patients
that entered the study 147 (90.7 %) completed the end of
treatment questionnaires, 144 (88.9 %) completed the 1-year
follow-up (MRI, questionnaires, physical examination).
All baseline variables were equally distributed in the
placebo and antibiotic groups (Table 2). The only exception
was the volume of Modic changes, where the placebo group
had significantly more minute changes (grade 1).
There were no significant differences in age and gender
between the 1-year participants and those lost to follow-up;
however, there were significantly more smokers amongst
those lost to follow-up.
The antibiotic group improved on all primary outcome
measures and improvement continued from 100 days follow-
up until 1-year follow-up. In comparison to the placebo group,
the 1-year improvement was both statistically significant on all
outcome measures and clinically important in terms of the
relative magnitude of improvement for the primary outcome
measures (Tables 3, 4). There were no difference between the
groupsintheserumanalysisatbaselineorfollow-up(Table 5).
Patients reported that pain relief and improvement in dis-
ability commenced gradually, for most patients 6-8 weeks
after start of the antibiotic tablets and for some at the end of
the treatment period. Improvements reportedly continued
long after end of the treatment period, at least for another
6 months, and some patients reported continuing improve-
ment at 1-year follow-up.

Randomization was performed by the Central Pharmacy,
Odense University Hospital using a computer-generated
randomization list retained at the pharmacy until after the last
patient's 1-year follow-up. Placebo tablets were calcium
carbonate and identical in size, color, coating and aluminum
packing to the active tablets. All tablets were packed in sealed
white cardboard boxes on which only the patient number was
printed (1-162). Patients and the assessor were blinded to
randomization until after completion of the patient's 1-year
follow-up. Patients were recommended not to seek any other
treatment during the 1-year follow-up period. At both follow-
up treatments by doctors, physiotherapists and alternative
treatment providers were registered.
Three independent experts in infectious diseases were
presented with the bacterial culture results of Stirling's study
[10] and all three recommended amoxicillin-clavulanate.
This drug is known to be able to penetrate into the discs [26].
Therefore, treatment consisted of amoxicillin-clavulanate
(500 mg/125 mg) (Bioclavid ) tablets three times a day, at
8 h intervals, for 100 days. This long duration of antibiotic
treatment is commonly prescribed for post-operative discitis.
The randomization divided patients into four dosage
groups: A (n = 45) one Bioclavid tablet, B (n = 36) one
placebo tablet, C (n = 45) two Bioclavid tablets, D
(n = 36) two placebo tablets. Compliance was measured in
daily medication diaries. During their 12-month participa-
tion in this trial patients were not provided with any other
treatment except mild analgesics, if required.
Study flow
At both baseline and at 1-year follow-up each participant
underwent a physical examination and completed self-repor-
ted questionnaires. An MRI and blood samples were also
taken. The MRI protocol at baseline and at the 1-year follow-
up were uniform and performed by the same staff, blinded to
treatment, and in the same MRI machine. At the end of the
treatment period, (100 days), patients were also mailed a
questionnaire. The patients and the observer were blinded to
the allocation and all previous measurements. All physical
examinations were performed by the same blinded observer.
At baseline, all patients had a 1.5 h thorough patient
education session including important information about;
what are Modic changes? Why are they so painful? What is
the presumed pathoanatomical pathway for the link
between the previous herniation and the present Modic
type 1 changes? Why they should not do exercise during
the treatment period and so forth. All patients were allowed
to take their usual anti-inflammatory and pain relieving
medication (treatment as usual).
To avoid a later need for imputation, the project secre-
tary checked every questionnaire for completion, if missing
data, the patient was asked to fill in before leaving the
center. A project secretary, also blinded to treatment allo-
cation, entered all data in EpiData v3.1 (The EpiData
Association, Odense, Denmark), coded under the partici-
pant's project number.
Outcome measures
All patients underwent clinical examination and blood tests
(serum analysis) at baseline and at end of treatment. Self-
reported questionnaires were completed at baseline; end of
antibiotic treatment (100 days), and at 12-month follow-up.
The outcome measures are presented in Table 1.
The primary outcome measures were disease-specific
disability Roland Morris Questionnaire [27] (RMDQ) and
lumbar pain [28] (LBP Rating Scale). A clinically impor-
tant change was defined as a 30 % reduction of the indi-
vidual's baseline score and 2 LBP rating scale points [29]
(Table 1). Secondary outcome measures were global per-
ceived effect, leg pain, hours with LBP during the last
4 weeks, EQ-5D Thermometer, days with sick leave,
bothersomeness, constant pain, MRI Modic grading, serum
analysis, four test at the physical examination.
Sample size
Power calculations were based on the results of a pilot
study, where the patients receiving antibiotics had a med-
ian reduction of RMDQ of 3.7 [24]. A sample size of 65 in
each group was calculated as necessary to detect a reduc-
tion of minimum 3.7 in the antibiotic group on the RMDQ,
with a SD of the difference of four and a placebo effect of
1.4 on the RMDQ, for an alpha of 0.05 and a power of 0.90.
Dropout due to side effects was estimated to be 10 %. The
sample size calculation is based on a two-group compari-
son hence comparing antibiotics with placebo is the main
aim. To fulfill a late request from the Danish Medical
authorities a dose-response part was included, but the
study is not designed for this tertiary purpose and therefore
this is not formally tested.
Statistics
All statistics were performed by an independent professor
in statistics at Aalborg University who was blinded to
group allocation. Data were analyzed in STATA version
16.

1|Differences in binary variables were tested with Fisher's
2|exact test. Continuous data were analyzed with three tests.
3|Firstly, crude an unpaired T-tests; secondly, adjusted for
4|gender and age. Thirdly, if the distribution was not nor-
5|mally distributed, with the Mann-Whitney test. No interim
6|analysis was performed. Analyses were preformed on all
7|patients who participated at the 1-year follow-up and all
8|patients were analyzed in their 'intention to treat' group,
9|regardless of their compliance to the medicine protocol.
10|Ethics
11|The study was approved by and registered in: the Danish
12|Medicine Agency and the Scientific Ethics Committee of
13|the Region of Southern Denmark (no. S-VF-20050112),
14|the Danish Data registry, Euro-dract (2005-005500-17),
15|Government Clinical trial registry (NCT00302796) and
16|monitored by the Unit of Good Clinical Practice (GCP),
17|University of Southern Denmark. All patients signed a
18|written informed consent prior to participation.
19|Results
20|The study flow chart is shown in Fig. 1. Of the 162 patients
21|that entered the study 147 (90.7 %) completed the end of
22|treatment questionnaires, 144 (88.9 %) completed the 1-year
23|follow-up (MRI, questionnaires, physical examination).
24|All baseline variables were equally distributed in the
25|placebo and antibiotic groups (Table 2). The only exception
26|was the volume of Modic changes, where the placebo group
27|had significantly more minute changes (grade 1).
28|There were no significant differences in age and gender
29|between the 1-year participants and those lost to follow-up;
30|however, there were significantly more smokers amongst
31|those lost to follow-up.
32|The antibiotic group improved on all primary outcome
33|measures and improvement continued from 100 days follow-
34|up until 1-year follow-up. In comparison to the placebo group,
35|the 1-year improvement was both statistically significant on all
36|outcome measures and clinically important in terms of the
37|relative magnitude of improvement for the primary outcome
38|measures (Tables 3, 4). There were no difference between the
39|groupsintheserumanalysisatbaselineorfollow-up(Table 5).
40|Patients reported that pain relief and improvement in dis-
41|ability commenced gradually, for most patients 6-8 weeks
42|after start of the antibiotic tablets and for some at the end of
43|the treatment period. Improvements reportedly continued
44|long after end of the treatment period, at least for another
45|6 months, and some patients reported continuing improve-
46|ment at 1-year follow-up.

8|There was a trend towards a positive dose-response rela-
9|tionship with double dose antibiotics appearing to be more

12|shown). For a 30 % or more reduction [29] in baseline
13|disease-specific disability (RMDQ), the 'number needed to
14|treat' in the single-dose group was 4.0 (95 % CI 2.1-11.8)
15|and for the double dose group was 3.0 (95 % CI 1.9-5.8).
16|For the arbitrary threshold of a 100 h reduction in 'painful
17|hours in the last 28 days' the number needed to treat in the
18|single-dose group was 3.0 (95 % CI 1.6-3.9) and for
19|double dose group was 2.0 (95 % CI 1.4 to 2.7).
20|Unintended effects
21|Adverse events were more common in the antibiotic group
22|(65 % of participants) compared to the placebo group
23|(23 %). These were mainly low-grade gastroenterological
24|complaints such as loose bowel movements, increased
25|flatus or burping. Middle-grade events were defined as
26|loose bowl movements lasting more than 3 weeks and were
27|reported by 27 % in the antibiotics group and 11 % of
28|those in the placebo group, considerable side effects in 21
29|and 6 %, respectively. One case of a serious adverse
30|(severe vomiting resulting in blood in the vomit) event was
31|reported in the placebo group and none in the antibiotic
32|group. No difference in the number of adverse effects was
33|observed between the double and single-dose antibiotics.

answers.justification: Approved scope is one-year RMDQ among all randomized participants, antibiotic combined-dose versus placebo combined-dose; assignment effect. The report says 144/162 (88.9%) completed one-year follow-up (page 4) and flow chart breaks this down as 77/90 antibiotic (85.6%) and 67/72 placebo (93.1%), while the analyzed follow-up table reports those same denominators and median RMDQ values 7 versus 14 (page 7). Thus 18/162 lack follow-up, materially below near-complete ascertainment; the 5.7 antibiotic abstract value conflicts with detailed table value 7.0 but both refer to followed participants, so missing outcomes remain consequentially unresolved. ITT-group analysis applies only to one-year participants, not all randomized.

Outcomes for 18 participants without one-year follow-up and their relation to true RMDQ values are unknown.

counterevidence.implication: 144 completed one-year questionnaire follow-up; 88.9% is not nearly all for this continuous outcome and smokers were more frequent among those lost.
